variables.content: An observed discrepancy between the theoretical transition-state-theory (TST) rate constant computed using gas-phase barriers and the larger experimental second-order rate constant measured in reactor experiments corresponds to an effective free-energy lowering of approximately 3.0 kcal·mol⁻¹, and this magnitude of discrepancy is attributed primarily to heterogeneous effects (stabilization or catalysis by reactor surfaces, such as increased surface area enhancing formation or stabilization of asymmetric dimers) rather than to errors in the gas-phase electronic energies or in the idealized kinetic model used for the TST estimate.

In comparing catalysed (tin(II) oxide present) and uncatalysed (blank, no solid catalyst) batch runs, the observed initial reaction rate r_{obs} in the catalysed experiment is modelled as the arithmetic sum of an independent homogeneous uncatalysed rate r_{uncat} (measured in blank runs) and a heterogeneous catalysed surface rate r_{het}, i.e. r_{obs}=r_{uncat}+r_{het}; the proposition is that in the low‑conversion initial regime (conversion < 10%) the two pathways do not interact nonlinearly, so that subtracting the measured r_{uncat} from r_{obs} yields the intrinsic heterogeneous rate r_{het} used for kinetic parameter estimation.

The high cyclohexane conversion and very high cyclohexanol selectivity observed when using the calcined CoHMA catalyst under the defined reaction conditions (50 mg catalyst, 18 mmol cyclohexane, 5 mmol 2‑butanone, 18 mmol 30 wt% H2O2, 10 mL acetic acid, reflux 80–110 °C) are attributed primarily to catalysis at heterogeneous framework‑stabilized cobalt sites in the solid CoHMA material rather than to catalysis by cobalt species leached into the reaction solution that operate as homogeneous catalysts; this attribution assumes that the preliminary single recycling experiment (first reuse: 86% conversion and 89% selectivity) together with the absence of obvious homogeneous‑product signatures in the product analysis are sufficient to exclude a dominant homogeneous contribution during catalysis.

Within the heterogeneous catalysis literature available before 3 February 1995, no published study had reported that application of microwave energy to a catalytic reaction changed the identity of the product species formed, as distinct from changing only reaction rate, conversion, or selectivity among an unchanged set of products.

For a heterogeneous reaction on a supported catalyst in which the conversion of inlet carbon monoxide ($CO$) to measured hydrocarbon products is approximately $1\%$ (conversion defined here as the mole fraction of feed $CO$ consumed to form hydrocarbons during the experiment), and where "primary selectivity" is defined as the distribution of hydrocarbons formed directly from the first surface reaction events before any secondary re-adsorption and further surface transformation of those primary products, the rates of secondary re-adsorption and of subsequent homologation or isomerization reactions are negligible compared with the rate of primary product formation under static experimental conditions at $176\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 760 Torr reported for the $CO+H_{2}$ experiments, so that the measured C$_1$–C$_5$ product distribution can be treated as an approximation to the primary selectivity.

An auxiliary control experiment in which reaction tubes were packed with calibrated fused-silica/helical quartz elements (quartz helices) so as to increase internal surface area by approximately six-fold is taken to demonstrate that the measured first-order rate constants are essentially independent of heterogeneous internal surface area under the sealed-tube experimental protocol described, and therefore that heterogeneous surface-mediated catalysis or surface-propagated radical-chain pathways are not operative to a significant extent in the sealed-tube kinetic measurements reported here.
      [32],[33]

If two catalytic transformations measured under the same experimental conditions exhibit indistinguishable reaction orders with respect to the same reactants and the same apparent activation energy within the stated experimental uncertainties, then those transformations share the same rate-determining elementary step under those conditions, i.e., identical kinetic orders and identical apparent activation energies are sufficient empirical signatures to identify a common rate-determining elementary event in heterogeneous catalysis in the absence of evidence for multiple competing rate-limiting pathways.

A mean‑field first‑principles microkinetic closure that computes heterogeneous reaction rates r_i from site‑averaged surface coverages θ_j and transition‑state‑theory rate expressions—i.e., rates r_i that depend only on averaged θ_j and gas‑phase partial pressures and that omit explicit lateral adsorbate–adsorbate interactions, nanoscale site heterogeneity, and spatial correlation terms—provides an adequate boundary closure for reactor‑scale particle‑resolved CFD of CO2 hydrogenation on the Cu‑based catalyst studied; specifically, neglecting lateral interactions and surface spatial correlations does not materially change predicted steady‑state surface coverages, local reaction rates, or reactor‑scale conversion and selectivity trends for the operating conditions and kinetic network considered.

If two structurally related substrates (for example DNM and 1‑BN) give different time profiles of product selectivity in the same heterogeneous catalytic reaction over FeS2, the analysis assumes that these differences principally reflect intrinsic differences in chemical reactivity (differences in elementary‑step rates and activation barriers on the catalyst surface) of the substrates rather than being driven mainly by differing physical properties such as volatility, differential solubility in the reaction solvent, differing rates of mass transfer between bulk and catalyst surface, or differing adsorption/desorption kinetics that could alter apparent selectivity time profiles without corresponding intrinsic reactivity differences.

The Low-Energy Electron Diffraction intensity-versus-voltage (LEED I–V) measurements reported for Rh(001), W(110) and Ti(0001) produce experimental interlayer-relaxation values that are substantially closer to values given by contemporary first-principles calculations cited in the literature; specifically, the LEED I–V results resolve the previously reported experiment–theory discrepancy for Rh(001) and W(110) and greatly reduce the discrepancy for Ti(0001).

The proposition: "Product selectivity in a heterogeneously catalyzed reaction (defined here as the fraction of consumed reactant carbon appearing as a given product) can vary with overall reactant conversion because sequential reactions, parallel pathways, and conversion-dependent rates alter product distributions as the reaction proceeds; therefore comparing selectivities between catalysts at the same fixed reaction time but at different conversions can confound intrinsic selectivity differences with conversion-dependent changes in product distribution unless selectivity–conversion relationships are reported or conversions are equalized for the comparison."

In a hot‑filtration (hot leaching) experiment the heterogeneous Pd@Cu(II)-MOF (2) was removed from the reaction mixture after 5 h under the optimized reaction conditions and the filtrate was allowed to continue under identical conditions for an additional 15 h; no further increase in benzyl alcohol conversion or in benzaldehyde selectivity was observed in the filtrate during that additional 15 h, demonstrating that catalytically active palladium species were not present in the reaction solution at levels sufficient to sustain the oxidation reaction and supporting a heterogeneous mode of catalysis.

The data-selection criterion applied to retain reactive experiments required that the independently measured heterogeneous wall-loss rate k_{w} be less than one half of the observed overall first-order rate k_{ex} (i.e., k_{w} < 0.5\,k_{ex}); it is assumed that meeting this criterion is sufficient to ensure that the residual bias from heterogeneous loss on the extracted bimolecular rate constants is negligible for the purposes of the reported Arrhenius fits and mechanistic interpretations.

If independently measured first‑order rate coefficients $k_1$ for the same substrate, temperature and initial pressure are statistically indistinguishable when the reaction is performed in two Pyrex vessels that differ in surface‑to‑volume ratio by a factor of 6 (one vessel with $S/V=1.0$, the other with $S/V=6.0$), then any heterogeneous wall‑catalyzed contribution to the observed rate is negligible compared to the homogeneous unimolecular contribution under those experimental conditions, because a heterogeneous surface process that contributed appreciably would produce a measurable dependence of $k_1$ on $S/V$.

The observed catalytic epoxidation activity and selectivity in reactions using hydrogen peroxide as oxidant under mild, solvent-free conditions are due predominantly to heterogeneous catalysis at active sites bound within or on the solid POM-intercalated, ionic-liquid-modified LDH particles (heterogeneous catalysis defined as catalytic turnover occurring at active sites bound to the solid), rather than being dominated by homogeneous catalysis arising from polyoxometalate species leached into the bulk reaction medium as dissolved molecular POM species during the reaction.

The catalyst designated 3, after activation and use in the described styrene oxidation protocol, retains catalytic activity and benzaldehyde selectivity over five consecutive reaction cycles with negligible loss in conversion; post-use powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of the recovered solid match the fresh catalyst pattern and thermogravimetric (TG) profiles of the reused material reproduce the fresh-sample thermal behavior (first-step dehydration at ≈393 K and decomposition at ≈573 K), and a hot-filtration experiment in which the activated solid catalyst was removed after 1 h of reaction and the filtrate was allowed to continue under the same conditions for the remaining 3 h shows no measurable further increase in conversion, collectively demonstrating heterogeneous catalysis and operational recyclability of 3 under the stated conditions.

The proposition is that the experimental observations reported to support matched versus mismatched catalyst–substrate pairs are based on a limited set of single‑timepoint conversion measurements (for example, reported examples include a mismatched experiment showing 10% conversion in one test and matched experiments showing approximately 50% conversion in related tests), and therefore the inference that differing instantaneous rates establish a general matched/mismatched kinetic model assumes that these snapshot conversion values are representative of the full time‑dependent kinetic profiles and of other substrates and conditions not explicitly examined; more comprehensive timecourse kinetic data would be required to quantify rate differences and selectivity across reaction time, concentration, and temperature.

In a liquid‑phase catalytic experiment carried out at elevated temperature, if the heterogeneous solid catalyst is removed by hot filtration (removal while the reaction mixture is maintained at reaction temperature) after a reaction interval and subsequent monitoring of the filtrate under the same reaction conditions shows only a conversion rate comparable to the blank (no catalyst) experiment, then the conclusion is that catalytically active species are not present in the filtrate in appreciable concentrations and the observed catalysis is heterogeneous rather than driven by homogeneous leached species.

Under the experimental regime used (microcatalytic operation at 300°C under hydrogen flow, measurements taken in a low-conversion regime where conversion was experimentally verified to be a linear function of reciprocal space velocity), the measured product selectivities expressed as percentages of converted substrate forming specific olefin isomers directly reflect the relative rates of competing elementary reaction channels operative at the rate-determining step; consequently, mechanistic inferences about whether the rate-determining step is concerted or stepwise can be drawn from the observed selectivity patterns in the first-pulse product distributions.

Given the experimentally extracted acoustic-phonon coupling coefficient $A=-0.90(5)\ \mathrm{MHz}\,\mathrm{K}^{-p}$ and a cited first-principles theoretical estimate for the same coefficient of approximately $A_{\mathrm{theory}}\approx-0.03\ \mathrm{MHz}\,\mathrm{K}^{-4}$ (the theoretical estimate and its computational basis are those reported by Allen and Nery), the large numeric mismatch (a factor on the order of 30 between experiment and theory) indicates that current first-principles theoretical treatments likely do not fully capture cancellation effects among different electron–phonon coupling contributions relevant for the low-temperature band-gap shift, assuming that the experimental and theoretical definitions of $A$ and $p$ are directly comparable and that theoretical numerical uncertainties and omitted higher-order corrections are smaller than the stated factor-of-30 discrepancy.
